item.title: Chinese EV connects German drivers, opens doors to greater cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
While German brands remain firmly established in the domestic market, the country's roads are becoming more diverse, with European and Asian manufacturers gaining ground. Chinese EV brands, in particular, are becoming increasingly visible. REGENSBURG, Germany, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- On Oct. 3, Germany's Unity Day, German software engineer Renick Buettner set off in his NIO EL7, an electric SUV made by Chinese automaker NIO, for the Bavarian city of Regensburg, where NIO owners gather on a Saturday each month to share their experiences and enthusiasm for the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) brand. At 27, Buettner grew up in Germany's car-loving culture and has driven a range of European and American brands. Today, however, two Chinese electric vehicles have found a place in his garage. What won him over was not simply the price or the brand, but how naturally the cars fit into his daily life. "I want a simple, intelligent experience," Buettner told Xinhua during the drive. As the automotive industry shifts toward electrification and intelligent mobility, his priorities have evolved, with software, intelligent cockpits and ease of use becoming increasingly important. "Many of the smart features in Chinese electric vehicles are seamlessly integrated into the driving experience. They simplify tasks that would otherwise require manual operation and make the car a more natural part of everyday life," he said. His impressions are based on firsthand experience. During a road trip to China this spring, Buettner attended events showcasing new models from Chinese automakers and test-drove several vehicles. He was particularly impressed by their interior design and intelligent features, which he found offered a different approach from that of German brands. For instance, drivers can use navigation systems to locate specific types of charging stations, control vehicle functions through voice commands and adjust the air conditioning with an intelligent in-car assistant. "Once you have been to China and driven these cars yourself, you see things differently," he said. Buettner's experience reflects a broader shift in Germany, a country long renowned for its automotive engineering and home to some of the world's leading carmakers. While German brands remain firmly established in the domestic market, the country's roads are becoming more diverse, with European and Asian manufacturers gaining ground. Chinese EV brands, in particular, are becoming increasingly visible. By the time Buettner arrived in Regensburg, around 20 Chinese-made electric vehicles had gathered at the meeting venue. Their owners shared a common interest in Chinese cars, swapping stories about the convenience of battery swapping, souvenirs from trips to China and road journeys across Europe, including to Norway and the Netherlands. For Andreas Tasch, 54, head of an IT consulting company in Munich, the appeal goes beyond digital features. Having driven a Chinese electric vehicle for three years, he particularly appreciates its software, intelligent cockpit and the ecosystem of services built around it. "I often drive long distances to visit my family. There happens to be a battery-swapping station along the way. I can drive in, have the battery replaced in just three or four minutes and continue my journey," he said. "Passengers who experience it for the first time are often amazed." Tasch sees the development of intelligent vehicles as opening up new opportunities for cooperation between German and Chinese automakers. The two sides have complementary strengths, as German manufacturers bring expertise in vehicle hardware, engineering and design, while Chinese companies have made significant advances in software, batteries and supply chain management, he said. "Combining these strengths in batteries, charging infrastructure, university research and engineering could create great opportunities," he added. Such views are increasingly shared by industry leaders. Hildegard Mueller, president of the German Association of the Automotive Industry, noted the rapid innovation in China's automotive sector and called on Germany and China to build on their longstanding cooperation and deepen exchanges in standards, technology, infrastructure and data amid global industry shifts and supply chain uncertainties. The growing presence of Chinese automakers in Europe is also creating fresh momentum for industrial cooperation. The relationship is moving beyond vehicle exports toward a broader range of activities, including joint research and development, technology exchange, local manufacturing and supply chain partnerships. At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, which recently concluded, 16 Chinese automakers showcased 25 brands, marking a record level of participation. Among them were Leapmotor, Geely, GAC and XPeng. Serge Gachot, director of the Paris Motor Show, said Chinese companies were increasingly looking beyond product displays to establish long-term partnerships with local businesses. ■

item.title: Economic Watch: Local industries give China's counties global reach
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
NANNING, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- Sun Kai made a surprising discovery in Central Asian supermarkets: small mandarins from China were a hit with local shoppers, who affectionately called them "baby mandarins." During visits to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Sun, 39, a sales manager at Guilin Jolly Cool Fruit Agricultural Products Co., Ltd., saw the fruit selling for as much as 60 yuan (about 8.93 U.S. dollars) per kilogram. "Their love for mandarins, especially the smaller varieties, exceeded our expectations," he said. For Xing'an County, Sun's hometown in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, overseas demand is delivering new opportunities to the citrus industry, a pillar of the local rural economy. The county has more than 200,000 mu (around 13,333 hectares) of citrus orchards, producing over 500,000 tonnes of fruit annually, according to local reports. Sun began exploring overseas markets in 2023 after years in domestic e-commerce and fruit processing. Nanfeng mandarins, a widely grown variety in Xing'an, have proved popular in Central Asia. Newer varieties have pushed down their prices at home, but their small size, sweetness and juiciness appeal to overseas consumers. With support from local authorities, Sun's company worked with village committees to register orchards collectively, helping smaller growers enter overseas markets. The company's export value rose from roughly 500,000 U.S. dollars in 2023 to several million U.S. dollars in 2025, Sun said. Sun estimated that some farming households could earn a combined 50,000 to 60,000 yuan annually from citrus growing and seasonal work in harvesting, sorting and packaging. More than 40,000 households in Xing'an have benefited from citrus exports, while the county's citrus industry is expected to generate over 1.1 billion yuan in output value this year. In neighboring Quanzhou County, another local agricultural specialty is finding customers abroad. Anhe Town has grown taro for more than 1,000 years, aided by its mild climate and fertile soil. Today, the town has approximately 18,600 mu of taro fields, accounting for more than 60 percent of Quanzhou's total. The industry's annual output value has exceeded 100 million yuan for several consecutive years. You Wei, 47, chairman of a Quanzhou-based agricultural company, exports locally grown taro to Malaysia and the Republic of Korea. His company operates a cold-storage facility with a capacity of about 600 tonnes, thus allowing sales beyond the harvest season. "Demand for taro has grown in recent years, driven by increasing interest in healthy eating and the popularity of taro balls in bubble tea," You said. Xing'an and Quanzhou are among a growing number of Chinese counties building on their local strengths to reach overseas markets, aided by improving transportation and logistics networks. Products ranging from agricultural specialties and makeup brushes to wigs, power equipment, tires and toys are finding buyers abroad. In Luxi County in east China's Jiangxi Province, over 140 electric porcelain companies generated 16 billion yuan in revenue in 2025, with exports exceeding 380 million yuan. Meanwhile, Tianchang, a county-level city in east China's Anhui Province, has become one of China's three largest plush toy production bases, with more than 90 percent of local toy products exported to Europe and the United States. Counties contribute approximately 40 percent of China's GDP, according to a think tank report released in late 2025. The outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for developing county economies with distinctive local strengths, while the 2026 "No. 1 central document," the first policy statement issued by China's central authorities each year, emphasizes cultivating county-level industries that benefit rural residents. Qiu Tongwei, a professor at Nanjing Agricultural University in east China, said counties should build on their local strengths and pursue distinctive development paths rather than simply copy one another. Yet reaching global markets brings challenges, particularly for inland agricultural exporters facing long transport routes and the need to keep produce fresh. Sun recalled losing an entire truckload of fruit overseas after problems with temperature control and difficulties in communication with a driver. Fruit from Xing'an is generally shipped by sea through Shenzhen in south China or overland via the Horgos border crossing in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Sun hopes the Pinglu Canal, which opened to navigation in September, could eventually offer another shipping option to Southeast Asian markets. Sun plans to register more orchards and introduce more fruit varieties to overseas buyers. "We hope to take mandarins grown along the Xiangjiang River to consumers around the world," he said. ■

item.title: APEC host China's evolving role in regional economic cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
BEIJING, Nov. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the city of Shenzhen, located in south China's Guangdong Province, prepares to welcome Asia-Pacific leaders for the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting next week, China is set to host this gathering for the third time, marking another milestone in its decades-long engagement with regional economic cooperation. Over the past 25 years, east China's Shanghai, Beijing in north China and now Shenzhen have served as host cities, tracing the country's evolving role from a participant learning to align with international trade rules to an important contributor to regional cooperation and an increasingly active pioneer of new areas of growth. Looking back to 2001, when APEC leaders gathered in Shanghai, Asia was still recovering from the financial crisis of the late 1990s, and China was days away from joining the World Trade Organization (WTO). The Shanghai Accord that emerged from the meeting reaffirmed the Bogor Goals of free and open trade and investment. APEC leaders at that time also welcomed China's WTO accession. "At that time, China was still learning the rules of international trade and was preparing to become deeply integrated into the multilateral trading system centered on the WTO," said Lin Feng, an official of China's Ministry of Commerce. Since joining APEC in 1991, China had actively aligned itself with international rules to fit into this multilateral trading system. By the time it first hosted APEC in Shanghai, China's average tariff rate had fallen from 39.5 percent to 15.3 percent, while its trade with other APEC economies had nearly tripled. Following the Shanghai meeting, China continued to expand opening up and embed itself deeper in regional industrial and supply chains. In 2010, it became the world's second-largest economy. In 2014, China hosted the APEC economic leaders' meeting for a second time, with the event held in Beijing. One of the key outcomes was the endorsement of the Beijing Roadmap for APEC's Contribution to the Realization of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), marking a significant step toward advancing regional economic integration. "It was a substantive step toward the establishment of the FTAAP. Since then, APEC economies have steadily advanced related work toward this shared goal, with China playing an important leading role," said Zhou Yamin, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. In the years that followed, regional trade and economic integration gained further momentum, with the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement (DEPA) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) entering into force. The full implementation of the RCEP in 2023, in particular, brought into operation the world's largest free trade agreement by population and trade volume. "China's role in APEC has evolved from an important participant into a key contributor to the agenda and an active promoter of practical cooperation. It has not only helped shape the direction of APEC cooperation, but has also worked to advance grand blueprints amid complex realities, exerting a far-reaching influence on regional cooperation," said Zhang Jingjia, a researcher at Nankai University, located in Tianjin Municipality in north China. Over the past decade or so, APEC member economies, home to nearly 40 percent of the world's population, have come to generate more than 60 percent of global economic output and close to half of world trade, pulling the center of gravity of the global economy steadily toward the Asia-Pacific. China, notably, has served as a stabilizing anchor for regional economic growth. With its overall tariff level already reduced to 7.3 percent, approaching the average among developed economies, China has emerged as the largest trading partner of 13 APEC economies. In 2025, trade between China and other APEC members had grown to 1.4 times its 2018 level, accounting for around 60 percent of China's total foreign trade. By the end of 2025, China's outbound direct investment (ODI) stock in other APEC economies had reached 2.41 trillion U.S. dollars, which is more than 70 percent of the country's total ODI stock. Now, 12 years after its previous turn as host, China is once again chairing APEC. Working with other member economies under the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," China has focused on three priorities, namely openness, innovation and cooperation, and hosted more than 300 meetings and events across the country during the year. At a press conference earlier this month, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao called on APEC economies to uphold free trade and build an open, mutually beneficial model of development, promote innovation-driven growth with strengthened policy coordination on digital and intelligent trade rules, and work toward a fairer and more equitable international economic and trade order. Given a sluggish global economy, innovation is expected to become a new source of momentum for APEC cooperation and growth. "China's strengths in green and digital economy and artificial intelligence, together with its commitment to openness and cooperation, will create unprecedented opportunities for other APEC economies," Zhou said. Across electronics, automobiles and equipment manufacturing, China and other APEC economies are building complementary and mutually reinforcing innovation chains. A growing number of Asia-Pacific and global multinationals have established research and development centers in China, using its vast market to rapidly deploy and iterate new technologies. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's high-tech products trade with other APEC economies surged 50.3 percent year on year to 6.66 trillion yuan (about 991.78 billion U.S. dollars), contributing almost half of the total bilateral trade increase. China's push for innovation-driven growth, via technology advancement and industrial integration, will expand the overall pie of Asia-Pacific trade and investment, experts said, noting that its own development can help drive shared growth across the Asia-Pacific and inject fresh momentum into the region. ■

item.title: China willing to further boost political mutual trust with Thailand, says Chinese premier
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-14
Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) BANGKOK, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Friday that China is willing to work with Thailand to further consolidate the foundation of political mutual trust, support each other's core interests and major concerns, tap cooperation potential in various fields and deliver more tangible results to better benefit the peoples of both countries. Li made the remarks when meeting with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. He said Chinese President Xi Jinping met with Anutin during the Thai PM's official visit to China in July, and the two leaders jointly charted the course for the development of China-Thailand relations. Li said that, with his visit to Thailand, the prime ministers of the two countries have exchanged visits within four months, fully demonstrating the high level of bilateral relations. Noting that both China and Thailand are at an important stage of national development, Li said China firmly supports the Thai government in smoothly carrying out its work. China is willing to work with Thailand to make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers and the joint committee on economic and trade cooperation, Li said. China stands ready to work with Thailand to strengthen the alignment of development strategies, advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and key projects such as the China-Thailand railway, and accelerate consultations on a new five-year plan for economic and trade cooperation, Li said. He added that China is ready to promote the early realization of mutual protection of geographical indication products, and expand cooperation in such fields as finance, new energy, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence, so as to achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes at a higher level. China is ready to import more quality products from Thailand and encourages Chinese companies to invest and do business in the Southeast Asian country, he said, adding that China hopes the Thai side will provide a fair, stable and predictable business environment for Chinese companies. The two sides, Li said, should also strengthen exchanges and cooperation in areas including disaster prevention and mitigation, water resources management, education, tourism and media, and step up efforts to combat illegal and criminal activities, to enhance the people's sense of gain from China-Thailand cooperation. At present, the international situation remains fraught with instability and uncertainty, Li said, noting that China is willing to strengthen coordination and cooperation with Thailand under multilateral frameworks including China-ASEAN, the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation, the United Nations, the World Trade Organization and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, so as to contribute to global peace and development. For his part, Anutin said Thailand attaches great importance to its relations with China and is committed to advancing all-round cooperation between the two countries and continuously elevating the Thailand-China comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership to new heights, bringing greater benefits to the two peoples. Thailand is willing to strengthen high-level exchanges with China, make good use of mechanisms such as the "2+2" strategic dialogue between foreign and defense ministers of the two countries, expand bilateral trade, and deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in fields including agriculture, finance, connectivity, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, e-commerce, and science and technology, said the Thai prime minister. Thailand is ready to continue providing a favorable business environment for Chinese enterprises investing in Thailand, strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation with China to combat online gambling, telecom and online fraud among other crimes, ensure the safety of Chinese tourists, and deepen people-to-people and cultural exchanges to consolidate the foundation of public friendship, Anutin said. Thailand supports China's successful hosting of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and stands ready to work with China to ensure the success of the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation Leaders' Meeting, making new contributions to regional stability, development and prosperity, said the Thai prime minister. Following the talks, the two leaders witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering the fields including the automotive industry, vocational education, agriculture, customs and security. ■ Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, Thailand, Nov. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Yin Bogu)

item.title: I will never forget you -- An American elder's cross-Pacific nostalgia for China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
* At 18, David bid farewell to Huangyuan with his family on a drizzly day. Thinking it was merely a short trip, they left their furniture and bedding sealed in the old house as they were -- no one imagined the farewell would stretch to 38 years. * David spent his childhood and adolescence in Huangyuan. More than three decades later, he returned to his "hometown" over 20 times, doing everything in his power to help the local people and leaving behind one touching story after another. * "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family." by Xinhua writers Wang Jinjin, Xie Tongqiang, Jiang Yi XINING, China, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- "Have you had dinner yet?" White-haired David Plymire spoke in fluent Huangyuan dialect, leaning toward the webcam in his living room in Springfield, Missouri. His greetings traveled across the Pacific, reaching Tongkhor Ancient Town in Huangyuan County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. "Yes, we have! We're waiting to see you on video!" David's longtime friend Wang Shikang replied from in front of the screen, eager to catch a glimpse of their old friend on the other end of the video call. David spent his childhood and adolescence in Huangyuan. More than three decades later, he returned to his "hometown" over 20 times, doing everything in his power to help the local people and leaving behind one touching story after another. CENTURY-OLD FRIENDSHIP In the 1920s, David's father, Victor Plymire, arrived in Tongkhor town along the ancient Tea Horse Road. In 1932, one-year-old David was brought to the small plateau town, where he spent the next 17 years growing up and came to regard it as his hometown. Time has taken its toll. The trans-Pacific journey has become too physically demanding for David over the past decade. "We all miss you! Almost ten years have passed since you were last able to come to Huangyuan. People here, young and old, miss you," Wang said, waving at him through the screen. Wang told David that they were making the video call from the ancient town's old streets, where many historic buildings had been restored with the help of photographs taken decades earlier by his father, Victor. A century ago, Victor took his camera around Tongkhor, documenting its streets, scenery and residents and leaving behind a unique visual record of life on the plateau. The photographs were later compiled into an album titled Imprint of a Legacy. Dong Baoming, general manager of Huangyuan Dancheng Tourism Development Co., Ltd., said Victor and David's photographs had helped bring the town's past back to life. The images now fill the Imprints exhibition hall, which has opened to the public, offering visitors a glimpse of Huangyuan as it once was. At 18, David bid farewell to Huangyuan with his family on a drizzly day. Thinking it was merely a short trip, they left their furniture and bedding sealed in the old house as they were -- no one imagined the farewell would stretch to 38 years. One moment during the call was particularly poignant. Bai Qiming, son of Bai Yongsheng, David's childhood friend known locally as "Ga Liang-ge," sent his greetings to David through the screen and spoke of how they had missed each other over the years. David fell silent for several seconds before quietly saying, "I can't come back now." TRANS-PACIFIC MEMORIES "Has the weather turned cold there?" David asked, then went on reminiscing about swimming in the town's river in summer and skating on the ice in winter when he was a boy. Memories came flooding back as David recalled how arduous travel had once been. A journey from Huangyuan to Xining took an entire day, with a stop at Zhamalong along the way for a bowl of noodles. "Do you have suanjiujiu (sea buckthorn)? Could you send me some suanjiujiu juice?" David asked with a childlike smile. Wang jokingly reminded David that he had sent him 3 kg of tsampa 15 years ago. David said he had carefully kept the package in his refrigerator ever since. He then recalled hand-grabbed mutton, pickled cabbage and Laba porridge. His longing for the familiar flavors of home and the warmth of everyday life back in Huangyuan went far beyond what the screen could convey. During the video call, David watched a prerecorded video of greetings from Huangyuan residents. Leaning back in his chair, he listened and watched attentively, looking closely at the familiar faces on the screen, sometimes breaking into hearty laughter. "My body is here, but my heart is in Huangyuan. I wish everyone back home peace and happiness," David said. As the conversation turned to shehuo, traditional festive performances held around the Chinese New Year, David spontaneously recited a children's rhyme from Huangyuan that he had known since boyhood: "On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, the temple gates swing open; village women come to light incense." ENDURING DEVOTION TO HOMETOWN David's correspondence with Wang, then director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, is preserved in the hospital's history exhibition hall. Several letters reveal a recurring subject: a CT scanner. In their early letters, the two addressed each other formally as "Director Wang" and "Mr. Plymire," discussing practical matters such as customs clearance. But with each of David's return visits to his hometown, the formality gradually melted away, giving rise to the warmer, more familiar terms "old friend" and "brother." Between 1997 and 1999, David made three trips to bring the CT scanner to Huangyuan. When the hospital could not afford the 500,000 yuan (75,000 U.S. dollars) tax bill, he rallied support to cover every penny. The scanner enabled the hospital's first brain surgery and helped save countless lives over its 15 years of service. Today, it rests in the hospital's history exhibition hall, alongside archival records documenting his many other contributions. "Mr. Plymire did more than simply donate a few pieces of equipment. He brought us a powerful source of inspiration," said Huang Jiong, director of Huangyuan County People's Hospital, visibly moved. He noted that David has tirelessly raised funds and mobilized support over the past three decades, helping secure donations of more than 30 pieces of medical equipment, worth a total of 6 million yuan (900,000 dollars). "My hometown has become part of who I am. My flesh and bones are the flesh and bones of Huangyuan," David said during the video call. Speaking about people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States, David slowly switched to English: "For two generations, my family has had a deep love for the Chinese people. This love has lasted for more than 100 years, from my father and mother to me. We love the people of China just as we love our own family." "Although I can no longer come back to visit because I am too old to travel by plane, I remember everyone. In my memories, I still walk along those streets, travel through the countryside, stand beside the rivers and talk with my friends," he said. "I shall always remember you in this life, and I will never forget you in the next." (Video reporters: Jiang Yi, Xie Tongqiang, Xie E, Zhao Yuhe, Zhang Long, Li Zhanyi; video editors: Yang Zeyi, Li Qin, Hui Peipei) ■

item.title: Xi stresses persevering with full, rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to provide strong guarantees for SOEs and state capital to get stronger, do better, and grow bigger. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction on Party building in SOEs. He noted that Party building in SOEs has been strengthened and new progress has been made across the board since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012. Xi urged further efforts to uphold and strengthen the Party's overall leadership of SOEs, better integrate the Party's leadership into all links of corporate governance, advance in-depth integration of Party building with production and operation, foster high-caliber, professional teams, and build good conduct, enforce discipline and fight corruption. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and a member of the CPC Central Committee Secretariat, speaks at a meeting on Party building in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 13, 2026. An important instruction by Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, was conveyed at the meeting held in Beijing on Friday. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei) The instruction was conveyed at a meeting on Party building in SOEs held in Beijing on Friday. Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and a member of the Secretariat of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event. Cai said Xi's important instruction has charted the course for further strengthening Party building in SOEs. Cai emphasized the need to accurately grasp the new requirements for Party building in SOEs arising from the evolving global, national and Party conditions. He called for efforts to resolutely combat corruption and further institutionalize and standardize the Party's leadership over SOEs. ■

item.title: Xi to attend APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, related events in Shenzhen
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-13
BEIJING, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping will chair the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting and deliver remarks, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced Friday. The meeting will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," the spokesperson said. The APEC CEO Summit will be held in Shenzhen from Nov. 17 to 18 under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the spokesperson said, adding that President Xi will attend the opening ceremony and deliver a keynote speech. President Xi will hold a welcome banquet for participating leaders and representatives, and hold bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the meeting, the spokesperson added. ■
